entities.summary:
Bartolomeo Mezzavacca (c. 1350, Bologna – 6 August 1396, Rome) was a prominent Italian cardinal and astute administrator whose career unfolded during the tumultuous early decades of the Western Schism (1378–1417), a period of profound ecclesiastical division that destabilized European politics and religious authority. Born into a Bolognese family, Mezzavacca rose through the ranks of the Church, first serving as Bishop of Rieti before assuming the influential Bishopric of Bologna, a key city within the Papal States. His life and actions illuminate the complex interplay between spiritual leadership, temporal power, and the shifting loyalties demanded by rival papacies.

Mezzavacca's ecclesiastical ascent began with his appointment as Bishop of Rieti by Pope Urban VI in 1378, the very year the Western Schism commenced. He was then elevated to cardinal-priest of San Marcello by Urban VI later that same year, marking him as a significant supporter of the Roman obedience. However, demonstrating the fluid allegiances characteristic of the era, he subsequently sided with the Avignonese Pope Clement VII, eventually serving as his legate in Bologna from 1383. This strategic shift positioned him at the heart of political and financial administration within a contested region, where he managed papal revenues and exerted considerable influence over local affairs until his death in 1396.
